name: Foundational API outages
blurb: Claims from enterprises whose core process halts when a third party model API is unavailable.
summary: Claims from enterprises whose core process halts when a third party model API is unavailable.

part_3_high_value_red_flags: A total exclusion for loss of use or interruption of computer services would remove the core claim.
A sublimit for business interruption liability of USD 100,000 per claim would be exhausted by a single enterprise customer.
An exclusion for failure to perform a contract or breach of express warranty would bar most SLA based claims.
A requirement that the outage be caused by physical damage to tangible property would exclude cloud or software failures.
A definition of covered damages that excludes consequential or indirect losses would eliminate customer revenue loss.
A retroactive date set after the API was first launched would exclude prior acts that later cause claims.
manuscript_wording_and_carve_backs: Delete the contractual liability exclusion to the extent the insured has assumed liability under a customer SLA that is scheduled to the policy.
Add a definition of covered damages that expressly includes customer business interruption losses and loss of use, not just direct physical loss.
Remove any requirement that an outage be caused by physical damage to covered property for the technology errors and omissions section.
Add a sublimit for regulatory fines and penalties arising from failure to meet uptime obligations in regulated sectors.
Negotiate a most favoured venue clause for claims brought by customers in multiple jurisdictions.
Carve back the failure to supply exclusion so that it does not apply to outages caused by the insured's own negligence in capacity planning.

part_4_program_structure_and_limits.bi_waiting_period: The business interruption waiting period is typically 8 to 12 hours for API providers because even short outages trigger customer credits, but this is negotiated based on the provider's own revenue loss per hour.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.business_interruption: Business interruption cover for the API provider's own lost revenue is written on a gross earnings basis with an extended period of indemnity of at least 90 days to capture customer churn after service restoration, and a contingent business interruption extension for failure of a critical cloud provider or power utility.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.property_eb_equipment: Electronic data processing equipment cover is written on a blanket basis for all owned and leased servers, storage arrays, and network switches, with a separate sublimit for transit and installation of new GPU hardware.
part_4_program_structure_and_limits.per_occurrence_primary_excess_layered_pr: The property program is layered with a primary layer covering physical damage to servers and networking equipment, and excess layers attach above a schedule of values that reflects replacement cost of GPU clusters, with per occurrence limits set by the maximum probable loss from a single data centre fire or flood.

part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.cgl_primary: Commercial general liability is occurrence-based but typically does not cover pure economic loss from service interruption, so it serves only as a backstop for bodily injury or property damage arising from an outage, with limits typically USD 1 million per occurrence and USD 2 million aggregate.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.paper_basis: Claims-made because the loss emerges when the customer reports the outage and alleges business interruption, often months after the API failure, and the policy must respond to claims first made during the policy period.
part_2_paper_type_and_limit_structure.excess_umbrella_towers: Excess umbrella towers sit above the technology errors and omissions policy rather than the CGL, and their attachment point is set by the underlying E&O limit, with tower height driven by the largest customer contract penalty rather than a fixed market figure.

part_1_core_third_party_liability_exposu: Breach of service level agreement causing customer revenue loss and contractual credits.
Negligent failure to maintain redundant API endpoints leading to prolonged outage.
Misrepresentation of uptime guarantees in marketing or customer contracts.
Failure to notify customers of planned maintenance causing avoidable downtime.
Inadequate capacity planning during model updates or traffic spikes causing cascading outages.
Liability for third party claims where a customer's downstream contracts impose penalties for non performance.

underwriter_wants_to_know: What is the maximum number of concurrent enterprise customers dependent on a single API endpoint?
What contractual liability has the insured assumed under customer SLAs for uptime and latency?
Does the API provider have redundant infrastructure across multiple cloud regions or data centres?
What is the historical frequency and duration of API outages over the past 36 months?
Are there any single points of failure in the model serving stack such as a single load balancer or GPU cluster?
What percentage of revenue comes from customers whose core process cannot function without the API?
